lessons.title: ChatGPT Tutorial for Beginners
objectives: Hold a working conversation with an AI chatbot rather than firing one-off questions at it
Recognise that a chat has a memory within it, and use that instead of repeating yourself
Decide what a chatbot is genuinely good at before you rely on it for anything
lessons.notes:
ChatGPT is a chatbot made by OpenAI. You type, it answers, and you keep going. That is the whole interface, which is why it spread so fast and also why most people stop at the shallow end of it.

The first thing to understand is that a chat is a CONVERSATION, not a search box. Everything you have said inside that one chat is still in front of the model, so you can say "shorter", "more formal", "now turn that into a WhatsApp message" without explaining yourself again. People who find AI frustrating are almost always treating each message as a fresh request. Start a NEW chat when you change topic entirely, and stay in the SAME chat while you are working on one thing.

The second thing: it answers in whatever shape you ask for. A table, a numbered list, an email, a script, a summary in Kiswahili. If you do not say, you get a wall of paragraphs, and then people conclude AI writes badly.

What it is genuinely good at: drafting, rewriting, summarising, explaining something you half-understand, restructuring messy notes, and getting you off a blank page. What it is not reliable at: current facts, specific numbers, prices, dates, laws, anyone's real details. The next module deals with that properly.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO — the features and the free limits shown in any tutorial go stale within months. What does not go stale is the habit: give it context, say what you want back, and keep the conversation going. Learn the habit, not the screen.
lessons.practice: Open a chat and give it a real task from your own week — an email you have been putting off, a set of notes to tidy up. Do not accept the first answer. Reply three times: once asking for it shorter, once asking it to change the tone, once asking for it in a different format. Notice that you never had to re-explain the task. That is the skill.

quiz.question: Why should you keep working in the same chat rather than starting a new one each time?
options: Everything already said in that chat stays available, so you can refine without re-explaining
New chats cost more money
The model answers faster in an older chat
Old chats are automatically deleted

quiz.question: Which of these is a chatbot LEAST reliable for?
options: Specific current facts, prices and dates
Rewriting a paragraph in a friendlier tone
Summarising notes you paste in
Explaining a concept you half-understand

lessons.title: Claude AI Tutorial for Beginners
objectives: Use a second AI assistant and notice where it differs in practice
Work with long documents by giving the assistant the source instead of describing it
Choose a tool by the job in front of you rather than by which brand you heard of first
lessons.notes:
Claude is an AI assistant made by Anthropic. Same idea as the last lesson — you type, it answers — and everything you just learned about conversations, context and asking for a format applies here unchanged. That is the point of doing two: the skill transfers, the brand does not.

Where it differs in daily use is worth knowing. Claude tends to hold long documents well, so the natural way to use it is to PASTE OR UPLOAD THE SOURCE and ask questions of it, rather than describing the document from memory and hoping. A contract, a long report, a tender document, twenty pages of meeting notes: put the thing in, then ask. It also tends to write in longer, more connected prose, which suits reports and explanations, where another tool might suit quick punchy copy.

The habit to build is comparative, not loyal. Run the same real task through two assistants and read both answers. You will form your own view of which one suits which job in about a week, and that view is worth more than any review.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO — do not memorise which model is best today. These tools leapfrog each other constantly, and any ranking in a tutorial is out of date by the time you watch it. What lasts is knowing HOW to evaluate one: give it a task you already know the right answer to, and see whether it gets there. That test works on every tool that has not been invented yet.
lessons.practice: Take the exact prompt you used in the last lesson and run it through Claude. Put the two answers side by side and write down one sentence on how they differ — not which is 'better', but what each one seemed to favour. Then do it once more with a long document: paste something over two pages in and ask three questions about it.

quiz.question: What is the most useful way to work with a long document in an AI assistant?
options: Paste or upload the document itself, then ask questions of it
Describe the document from memory and ask for a summary
Ask the assistant to find the document online
Type the document out one paragraph per message

quiz.question: Why is it a mistake to memorise which AI tool is 'the best'?
options: The tools change constantly, so the durable skill is knowing how to test one yourself
All AI tools produce identical output
Only one tool is available in Kenya
The best tool is always the most expensive one

lessons.title: Google Gemini: Tutorial for Beginners
objectives: Use an assistant that sits inside tools you already have open
Tell the difference between an answer drawn from the web and one drawn from the model
Check a cited source instead of trusting that a citation means the claim is true
lessons.notes:
Gemini is Google's AI assistant. The interesting thing about it for most people is not the chat window but WHERE IT SITS: inside the Google tools you are already in. That matters if your work already lives in Docs, Sheets, Gmail and Drive, because the friction of copying things in and out disappears.

The more important idea in this lesson is the difference between two kinds of answer.

An answer from the MODEL comes from what it learned during training. It is fluent, it is fast, and it has no idea what happened last week.

An answer that SEARCHES THE WEB fetches pages and answers from them. It can be current, and it can show you where it got each claim.

When an assistant gives you links, that is the second kind, and it is much better for anything factual — a price, a deadline, a rule, a current event. But note carefully what a citation does and does not prove. It proves the model found a page. It does not prove the page is right, and it does not prove the page actually says what the summary claims. Both of those failures are common.

So the working rule: for anything you will act on or repeat publicly, OPEN THE LINK. Reading one source takes thirty seconds and is the entire difference between using AI well and being embarrassed by it.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO — on a Kenyan data bundle, the cheap move is to let the AI do the wide search and then open only the one or two links that actually matter, rather than opening eight tabs yourself.
lessons.practice: Ask an AI assistant a question where the answer definitely changed recently — a current price, a recent rule change, a fixture. Get the answer with sources. Now open the top source and check two things: does the page say what the summary said, and is the page itself credible? Write down what you found. Do this three times and you will never fully trust a summary again, which is the correct state of mind.

quiz.question: What does a citation under an AI answer actually prove?
options: That the model found a page — not that the page is correct or says what the summary claims
That the claim has been fact-checked
That the answer is current
That the source is an official one

quiz.question: Which kind of question most needs an assistant that searches the web?
options: Anything factual and current, such as a price, deadline or rule
Rewriting a paragraph more politely
Explaining a general concept
Brainstorming names for a business

lessons.title: ChatGPT Image Generator Tutorial for Beginners
objectives: Describe an image in the terms a generator actually responds to
Iterate on a generated image instead of regenerating from scratch
Know where a generated image is and is not acceptable to use in paid work
lessons.notes:
Image generation follows the same law as text: the quality of what comes out tracks the specificity of what went in. "A shop" gives you a generic nothing. The parts a generator actually responds to are:

SUBJECT — what is in the frame, concretely. "A woman in her thirties arranging mandazi on a tray."

SETTING — where, and in what light. "Inside a small bakery, morning light through the doorway."

STYLE — photograph, flat illustration, watercolour, 3D render. Say it, or you get the generator's house style.

FRAMING — close-up, wide shot, from above, portrait or landscape shape.

MOOD — warm, clean, busy, calm.

Then ITERATE rather than reroll. Say what to change — "same image, but make the background less cluttered and shoot it from slightly lower" — instead of firing the same prompt again and hoping. Rerolling is the most common beginner mistake and it wastes both time and generations.

Two things it is still bad at, so plan around them: TEXT inside the image (signage, logos, labels come out mangled) and precise counts of things. If your design needs real text, generate the image clean and add the text yourself in Canva.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO — on paid client work, be careful. Generated images are fine for mockups, internal decks, social posts and concept boards. They are risky for anything claiming to show a real place, a real product or a real person, and misleading a customer with one is a genuine reputational problem. If a client asks for a photo of THEIR shop, take a photo of their shop.
lessons.practice: Write one prompt with all five parts — subject, setting, style, framing, mood — for an image you could actually use to promote something. Generate it. Then improve it with three change-requests in a row rather than rewriting the prompt. Save the first and last versions side by side; the gap between them is what iteration buys you.

quiz.question: What should you do when a generated image is close but not right?
options: Ask for specific changes to that image rather than running the same prompt again
Run the identical prompt repeatedly until one comes out well
Accept it, since generators cannot be steered
Switch to a different generator immediately

quiz.question: Which use of a generated image is genuinely risky in client work?
options: Presenting it as a photo of the client's real premises or product
Using it in an internal concept board
Using it as a background on a social post
Using it in a mockup for discussion

lessons.title: How to Chain Prompts for Accurate ChatGPT Responses
objectives: Break a large task into ordered steps instead of demanding it in one prompt
Check and correct the output of each step before the next one builds on it
Spot the point where a single prompt is being asked to do too much
lessons.notes:
Chaining means doing a big job in stages, checking each stage, and feeding the approved result into the next. It is the single biggest jump in output quality after basic prompting, and it costs nothing.

Why it works: every instruction you add to one prompt competes with the others for the model's attention. Ask for research, structure, drafting and polish in one message and each gets a quarter of the effort. Ask for them in four messages and each gets full effort — AND you get to correct the mistake at step one before it has been built on three times.

A worked example. Instead of "write me a 1,200-word article about starting a poultry business in Kenya":

STEP 1 — "List the ten questions a first-time poultry farmer in Kenya actually needs answered." Read it. Cut three, add two of your own.

STEP 2 — "Using those questions, draft an outline with section headings." Reorder it yourself.

STEP 3 — "Write section two only, 200 words, plain language." Fix it. Then section three.

STEP 4 — "Here is the full draft. Tighten it and flag anything that reads as a claim I should verify."

You stayed in control at every step, and every error was caught while it was still cheap to fix.

The tell that you should have chained: the output is long, superficially fine, and you cannot say what is wrong with it. That is what one overloaded prompt produces.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO — the check between steps is not optional, it IS the technique. Chaining without reading each step is just a slower way to get the same mediocre result.
lessons.practice: Take something you would normally ask for in one prompt and do it in four steps instead, correcting the output at each step before moving on. Keep both versions. Then answer one question honestly: at which step did you catch something that the one-shot version would have carried all the way to the end?

quiz.question: Why does splitting a task into chained prompts improve quality?
options: Each step gets full attention, and errors are caught before later steps build on them
The model charges less per message
Short prompts are processed more accurately than long ones in general
It forces the model to search the web

quiz.question: What is the sign that a task should have been chained?
options: A long output that seems fine but you cannot say what is wrong with it
The model refuses to answer
The output is too short
The model asks a clarifying question

lessons.title: How to Build a Custom GPT in ChatGPT (Beginner Tutorial)
objectives: Turn a prompt you reuse constantly into a saved, reusable assistant
Write instructions that hold across every future conversation
Judge honestly whether a task is repeated often enough to be worth saving
lessons.notes:
A custom GPT is a saved set of instructions plus optional reference files, so that a prompt you would otherwise retype every time is already loaded. The feature belongs to ChatGPT; other assistants have their own version of the same idea under a different name, and the thinking transfers.

What goes into the instructions is just your best prompt, written to last:

ROLE — who this assistant is. "You write product descriptions for a Nairobi thrift clothing shop."

RULES — the things you find yourself correcting every single time. "Never exceed 60 words. Always give the price in KSh. Never invent a measurement."

FORMAT — the exact shape of the output, every time.

REFERENCE FILES — your price list, your tone-of-voice examples, your past work. This is what lifts it from a saved prompt to something that actually knows your business.

The honest test before you build one: have you run this same task at least five times? Building assistants you use once is a very pleasant way to waste an afternoon, and beginners do it constantly.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO — there is real freelance money in this specifically, and it is a better sell than 'AI consulting'. Small businesses do not want to learn prompting; they want a thing that writes their listings correctly. Building someone a working custom assistant, loaded with their own price list and tone, and showing them how to use it, is a concrete deliverable with a concrete price. Module 8 picks this up.

One warning: whatever you upload as a reference file is inside that assistant. Do not load customer lists, ID numbers, or anything you would not email to a stranger.
lessons.practice: Find a prompt you have genuinely typed more than five times and turn it into a saved assistant: role, rules, format, and one reference file of your own good past work. Then test it on three real inputs. Every time the output needs correcting, do not fix the output — fix the instructions. Three rounds of that and it will be doing the job unattended.

quiz.question: What is the honest test for whether to build a custom assistant?
options: Whether you have already run the same task at least about five times
Whether the task is difficult
Whether you have a paid plan
Whether you have reference files to upload

quiz.question: When a saved assistant's output needs the same correction each time, what should you change?
options: The saved instructions, so the correction stops being needed
The output, each time by hand
The model being used
Nothing — some correction is unavoidable
